tips.startTitle: Start with just {{minutes}} minutes a day
tips.startBody: At age {{age}}, even {{minutes}} minutes of daily reading practice makes a huge difference. Try reading together at the same time each day — bedtime or after school works well. Consistency matters more than length.
tips.dailyTitle: Try to read every day — aim for {{minutes}} minutes
tips.dailyBody: You're already reading regularly, which is brilliant. Making it a daily habit — even for {{minutes}} minutes — will accelerate your child's progress noticeably. Little and often is the key.
tips.brilliantBody: Daily reading at age {{age}} is one of the best things you can do. Keep it up — {{minutes}} minutes a day is perfect. Your child is building strong reading foundations.
tips.bilingualBody: Speaking two languages at home is a huge advantage for your child's brain development. Keep speaking both languages — it doesn't slow down English reading. Read phonics books in English, but story books in either language.
tips.moreEnglishTitle: Extra English reading time will help
tips.moreEnglishBody: Since English isn't the main language at home, your child may need a little more daily phonics practice to build fluency. Try to fit in 10–15 minutes of English reading alongside your home language — both are valuable.
tips.dyslexiaBody: For children with dyslexia, phonics is especially important — and so is patience. Use the sound buttons, trace letters with fingers, and keep sessions short (5–10 minutes). Celebrate every small win. Progress may be slower but it's very real.
tips.speechBody: Children with speech and language needs benefit hugely from hearing sounds clearly. Use the sound buttons often, and give extra time for your child to respond. If they can hear the sound, they can learn to read it — even if speaking it is harder.
tips.ealTitle: Phonics works brilliantly for EAL learners
tips.ealBody: Systematic phonics is one of the most effective approaches for children learning English as an additional language. The sounds are consistent and predictable. Pair phonics practice with picture books to build vocabulary alongside decoding.
tips.adhdBody: Keep reading sessions to 5–8 minutes — shorter sessions with full attention beat longer distracted ones. Try adding movement: stand up between pages, use a pointer to track words, or do a star jump after each page. Make it active!
tips.gapTitle: Closing the gap is very achievable
tips.gapBody: Your child is a little behind UK expectations for their age — but this is completely normal and very fixable. With {{minutes}} minutes of daily phonics practice at Level {{level}}, most children catch up within a term. The key is regular practice, not cramming.
tips.homeschoolBody: As a homeschooling family, you have the advantage of one-to-one attention. Follow the levels in order — each book builds on the last. A short daily phonics session (10–15 minutes) followed by free reading works well.
tips.schoolSupportTitle: Phonics at home supports school learning
tips.schoolSupportBody: Your child's school may use a different reading approach. MyPhonicsBooks follows the UK phonics curriculum, which is systematic and evidence-based. Even 10 minutes at home will complement what they learn at school.
tips.headStartTitle: You're giving them a head start
tips.headStartBody: Starting phonics before school is a wonderful gift. Keep it playful — no pressure, just fun with sounds. Your child will arrive at school already confident with letters and sounds, which makes a real difference.
